Classification of classical and non-local symmetries of fourth-order nonlinear evolution equations Thanks: Supported by NSF-China grants 10671156 and 10771170.

Qing Huang, C. Z. Qu and R. Zhdanov 1. Department of Mathematics, Northwest University, Xi’an 710069,People’s Republic of China2. Center for Nonlinear Studies, Northwest University, Xi’an 710069,People’s Republic of China3. BIO-key International, 55121 Eagan, MN, USA ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: renat.zhdanov@bio-key.com
Abstract

In this paper, we consider group classification of local and quasi-local symmetries for a general fourth-order evolution equations in one spatial variable. Following the approach developed in [22], we construct all inequivalent evolution equations belonging to the class under study which admit either semi-simple Lie groups or solvable Lie groups. The obtained lists of invariant equations (up to a local change of variables) contain both the well-known equations and a variety of new ones possessing rich symmetry. Based on the results on the group classification for local symmetries, the group classification for quasi-local symmetries of the equations is also given.

Key words: Group classification, Symmetry group, Local symmetry, Quasi-local symmetry, Semi-simple algebra, Solvable Lie algebra, Fourth-order nonlinear evolution equation.

1. Introduction

The purpose of this article is to classify local and nonlocal symmetries of fourth-order evolution equations of the form

ut=F⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)​ux​x​x​x+G⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x).u_{t}=F(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx})u_{xxxx}+G(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}). (1)

Here FF and GG are arbitrary smooth functions and F≠0F\neq 0. Hereafter we adopt notations u=u⁡(t,x),ut=∂u/∂t,ux=∂u/∂x,ux​x=∂2u/∂x2u=u(t,x),\ u_{t}=\partial u/\partial t,\ u_{x}=\partial u/\partial x,\ u_{xx}=\partial^{2}u/\partial x^{2}, etc.

This paper is a farther development of the the methods classification approach suggested in [22] and successfully applied to various equations of mathematical and theoretical physics in [3, 4, 11, 12, 13, 22, 23]. It also generalizes the results of [12].

The class partial differential equations of Eq. (1) contains a number of important mathematical physics equations. Among the particular cases of Eq.(1) there are, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation

ut=−ux​x​x​x−ux​x−12​ux2,u_{t}=-u_{xxxx}-u_{xx}-\frac{1}{2}u_{x}^{2}, (2)

the extended Fisher-Kolmogorov (eFK) equation

ut=−ux​x​x​x+ux​x−u3+u,u_{t}=-u_{xxxx}+u_{xx}-u^{3}+u, (3)

the Swift-Hohenberg (SH) equation

ut=−ux​x​x​x−2​ux​x−u3+(κ−1)​u,κ∈𝐑.u_{t}=-u_{xxxx}-2u_{xx}-u^{3}+(\kappa-1)u,\ \ \kappa\in\mathbf{R}. (4)

It also contains the equation describing surface tension driven thin film flows

ut=−(u3​ux​x​x+f⁡(u,ux,ux​x))x,u_{t}=-\Big(u^{3}u_{xxx}+f(u,u_{x},u_{xx})\Big)_{x},

whose appropriate forms have been used to model fluid flows in physical situations such as coating, draining of foams, and the movement of contact lenses [16]. Another interesting particular case is the equation

ut=−(f⁡(u)​ux​x​x)x+(g⁡(u)​ux)x,u_{t}=-(f(u)u_{xxx})_{x}+(g(u)u_{x})_{x},

which appears in the context of surface dominated motion of thin viscous films and spreading droplets or plasticity (for further details, see, [5] and the references therein). If f⁡(u)=un,g⁡(u)≡0f(u)=u^{n},\ g(u)\equiv 0, it is the generalized lubrication equation. When n=3n=3, it is the capillary-driven flow. Equations with n<3n<3 can be used to describe slip models in the vicinity of u→0u\rightarrow 0. Another case of practical importance is n=1n=1, which describes the thickness of a thin bridge between two masses of fluid in a Hele-Shaw cell [7].

In [12], we perform preliminary group classification of the equations

ut=−ux​x​x​x+G⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x),u_{t}=-u_{xxxx}+G(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}), (5)

obtained from Eq.(1) by putting F=−1F=-1. Note that the so obtained lists of invariant equations contain equations (5) as particulars cases.

Lie symmetries play the central role in the modern theory of differential equations. One of the primary questions of theory of Lie symmetries is whether a given equation admits nontrivial symmetry. If the answer is positive one can apply the whole wealth of approaches utilizing symmetries to analyze and solve the equation in question. So that group classification of equations (1) is necessary first step in utilizing any symmetry methods and techniques. In the present paper, we perform preliminary group classification of Eq.(1) and describe all possible forms of the functions FF and GG such that Eq.(1) admit symmetry groups of the dimension n≤4n\leq 4.

The history of group classification methods goes back to Lie himself. In [14] he proved that a linear two-dimensional second-order partial differential equation (PDE) can admit at most three-parameter invariance group (apart from the trivial infinite-parameter symmetry group, which is due to linearity). The modern formulation of the problem of group classification of PDEs has been suggested by Ovsyannikov [17]. He introduced a regular method based on the concept of equivalence group (we will refer to it as the Lie-Ovsyannikov method). Ovsyannikov’s approach works at its best when the equivalence group of an equation under study is finite-dimensional and is not very efficient otherwise. So that the equations with arbitrary elements depending on two and more arguments cannot be efficiently handled with the Lie-Ovsyannikov method. To overcome this difficulty, Zhdanov and Lahno developed a different purely algebraic approach enabling to classify classes of PDEs having infinite-dimensional equivalence groups [22].

The method suggested in [22] has been applied to classify broad classes of heat conductivity [4], Schrödinger [24], KdV-type evolution [11], nonlinear wave [13], general second-order quasi-linear evolution [23], third-order nonlinear evolution [3] and fourth-order evolution [12] equations. Here we follow the approach of [22] in order to describe fourth-order nonlinear evolution equations (1) having non-trivial symmetry properties.

Our classification algorithm for local symmetries is a combination of the standard Lie infinitesimal algorithm, equivalence group and the structures of abstract Lie algebra. It consists of three major steps. We give a brief description of the steps involved. Further details can be found in [22].

The first step is to compute the most general symmetry group of (1) together with the classifying equations for FF and GG. In addition, we calculate the maximal local equivalence group admitted by Eq.(1) under consideration. The second step is essentially based on the explicit forms of commutation relations of low dimensional abstract Lie algebras [2, 18, 19]. Using these we construct all inequivalent realizations of symmetry algebras by basis infinitesimal operators admitted by Eq.(1). The third step is inserting the canonical forms of symmetry generators into the classifying equations, solving them, and deriving the invariant equations. Also we need to make sure that the corresponding symmetry algebras are maximal in Lie’s sense.

Since Lie symmetry is not always the best answer to all challenges of the modern theory of nonlinear differential equations, one has always been looking for ways to generalize it. A generalization is to allow for infinitesimals depending on the global behavior of the dependent variable, which is just the way the non-local symmetries arose. The most well studied non-local symmetries are those of linear PDEs [9, 10], while for those of nonlinear PDEs, much less is known. One possible approach has been suggested by Bluman [6, 8]. He derived non-local symmetries (potential symmetries) admitted by a given differential equation by realizing such symmetries as local symmetries of an associated auxiliary system. There is another way to constructing non-local symmetries which is to apply a non-local transformation to an equation admitting nontrivial Lie symmetries. Then some of Lie symmetries of the initial equation will remain Lie symmetries of the transformed equation, while the others become non-local ones, which are called quasi-local symmetries. The term quasi-local has been introduced independently in [1] and [15] to distinguish non-local symmetries that are equivalent to local ones through non-local transformation. It was noted in [4] that results of the group classification for local symmetries can be utilized to derive quasi-local symmetries of PDEs under study. Zhdanov and Lahno obtained some nontrivial examples of second-order evolution equations with quasi-local symmetries in [21]. recently, Zhdanov suggested a regular group-theoretical approach to the problem of classification of evolution equations that admit quasi-local symmetries [20].

The principal motivation for the present paper is a need for a unified group classification approach enabling to obtain both local/Lie and quasi-local/non-local symmetries of equations of the form (1). This approach is essentially based on the methods developed in the above mentioned papers [22, 20].

The outline of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, we obtain the classifying equations for the functions FF, GG and give the equivalence group of Eq.(1). In Section 3, we provide a detailed description of equations of the form (1) invariant with respect to semi-simple algebras. Section 4 is devoted to the classification of those evolution equations (1) which admit solvable Lie algebras. In Section 5, utilizing the results obtained while classifying for local symmetries, we derive the realizations of Lie algebras leading to equations admitting quasi-local symmetries.

2. Preliminary group analysis of Eq.(1)

In this section we derive the classifying equations for coefficients of ininitesimal operators of symmetry group of Eq.(1). Next, we obtain its most general equivalence group. It is a common knowledge that the Lie transformation group admitted by (1) is generated by the infinitesimal operators of the form

V=τ(t,x,u)∂t+ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂u,V=\tau(t,x,u)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u}, (6)

If there are no restrictions on FF and GG, then (8) should be satisfied identically, which is only possible when the symmetry group is the trivial group of identity transformations. Our goal is finding all specific forms of FF and GG for which Eq.(1) admits non-trivial symmetry groups. The basic idea, as suggested in [22], is to utilize the fact that for arbitrarily fixed FF and GG, all admissible vector fields form a Lie algebra. So that we can use the results of classification of abstract low-dimensional Lie algebras to construct all Lie symmetries of the form (7) admitted by (1). The next step is integrating the classifying equations, which yields the explicit form of the functions F,GF,\ G.

As a first step we need to compute the equivalence group of Eq.(1). To this end we have to construct all possible invertible changes of variables

t¯=T⁡(t,x,u),x¯=X⁡(t,x,u),u¯=U⁡(t,x,u),D⁡(T,X,U)D⁡(t,x,u)≠0,\bar{t}=T(t,x,u),\quad\bar{x}=X(t,x,u),\quad\bar{u}=U(t,x,u),\qquad\frac{D(T,X,U)}{D(t,x,u)}\neq 0,

which do not alter the form of Eq.(1). We present the final result of our calculations without detailed proof.

Proposition 2.

[3] The maximal equivalence group of Eq.(1) reads as

t¯=T⁡(t),x¯=X⁡(t,x,u),u¯=U⁡(t,x,u),\bar{t}=T(t),\quad\bar{x}=X(t,x,u),\quad\bar{u}=U(t,x,u), (9)

where T˙≠0\dot{T}\neq 0 and D⁡(X,U)D⁡(x,u)≠0\frac{D(X,U)}{D(x,u)}\neq 0.

We use equivalence transformation (9) to transform vector field (7) to a simplest possible (canonical) form.

Lemma 1.

Within the point transformation (9), vector field (7) is equivalent to one of the following canonical operators

∂t,∂x.\partial_{t},\qquad\partial_{x}. (10)
Proof.

Transformation (9) converts operator (7) into

V¯=τT˙∂t¯+(τXt+ξXx+ηXu)∂x¯+(τUt+ξUx+ηUu)∂u¯.\bar{V}=\tau\dot{T}\partial_{\bar{t}}+(\tau X_{t}+\xi X_{x}+\eta X_{u})\partial_{\bar{x}}+(\tau U_{t}+\xi U_{x}+\eta U_{u})\partial_{\bar{u}}.

The are two cases τ≠0\tau\neq 0 and τ=0\tau=0 to consider.

If τ≠0\tau\neq 0, choosing in (9) the function TT to satisfy τ​T˙=1\tau\dot{T}=1 and the functions XX and UU to be any two independent solutions of the equation

τ​Yt+ξ​Yx+η​Yu=0,Y=Y⁡(t,x,u),\tau Y_{t}+\xi Y_{x}+\eta Y_{u}=0,\qquad Y=Y(t,x,u),

leads to the canonical form ∂t\partial_{t}.

Suppose now that τ=0\tau=0 and ξ2+η2≠0\xi^{2}+\eta^{2}\neq 0 (otherwise operator (7) vanishes identically), then (7) is transformed to

V¯=(ξXx+ηXu)∂x¯+(ξUx+ηUu)∂u¯.\bar{V}=(\xi X_{x}+\eta X_{u})\partial_{\bar{x}}+(\xi U_{x}+\eta U_{u})\partial_{\bar{u}}.

If ξ≠0\xi\neq 0, then choosing in (9) a particular solution of ξ​Xx+η​Xu=1\xi X_{x}+\eta X_{u}=1 as the function XX and a fundamental solution of ξ​Ux+η​Uu=0\xi U_{x}+\eta U_{u}=0 as UU, transforms (7) into ∂x\partial_{x}.

If ξ=0,η≠0\xi=0,\ \eta\neq 0, by making the transformation (9) with t¯=t,x¯=u,u¯=x\bar{t}=t,\ \bar{x}=u,\ \bar{u}=x, we get the case ξ≠0\xi\neq 0, which has been already considered.

It is straightforward to verify that there is no transformation (9) which can transform ∂t\partial_{t} and ∂x\partial_{x} into another. ∎

Consequently, we have two inequivalent realizations of one-dimensional symmetry algebras ∂t\partial_{t} and ∂x\partial_{x}. Integrating the classifying equations for each symmetry operator yields the corresponding inequivalent equations of class (1).

In what follows, we use the notation Ak.i=⟨V1,V2,⋯,Vk⟩A_{k.i}=\langle V_{1},V_{2},\cdots,V_{k}\rangle to denote a kk-dimensional Lie algebra with basis elements ViV_{i} (i=1,2,⋯,k)(i=1,2,\cdots,k), the index ii standing for the number of the class to which the given algebra belongs.

Theorem 1.

There are two inequivalent equations (1) invariant under one-parameter symmetry groups:

A11=⟨∂t⟩:ut=F⁡(x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)​ux​x​x​x+G⁡(x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x),A21=⟨∂x⟩:ut=F⁡(t,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)​ux​x​x​x+G⁡(t,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x).\begin{array}[]{ll}A^{1}_{1}=\langle\partial_{t}\rangle:&u_{t}=F(x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx})u_{xxxx}+G(x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}),\\[5.69054pt] A^{2}_{1}=\langle\partial_{x}\rangle:&u_{t}=F(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx})u_{xxxx}+G(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}).\end{array}

Here FF and GG are arbitrary smooth functions. Furthermore, the associated symmetry algebra is maximal in Lie’s sense.

3. Classification of equations invariant under semi-simple Lie algebras

In this section, we classify all the equations of the form (1) admitting semi-simple Lie algebras. The lowest order real semi-simple Lie algebras are isomorphic to one of the following two three-dimensional algebras:

𝑠𝑜⁡(3):[V1,V2]=V3,[V1,V3]=−V2,[V2,V3]=V1;𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ):[V1,V2]=2V2,[V1,V3]=−2V3,[V2,V3]=V1.\begin{array}[]{cl}{\it{so}}(3):&[V_{1},V_{2}]=V_{3},\ [V_{1},V_{3}]=-V_{2},\ [V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1};\\[5.69054pt] {\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}):&[V_{1},V_{2}]=2V_{2},\ [V_{1},V_{3}]=-2V_{3},\ [V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1}.\end{array}

We begin by studying realizations of the algebras so(3) within the class of operators (7).

Taking into account of our preliminary classification, we can assume without any loss of generality that one of the basis operators, say V1V_{1}, is reduced to one of the canonical forms ∂t\partial_{t} and ∂x\partial_{x}.

Let V1=∂tV_{1}=\partial_{t} and V2V_{2}, V3V_{3} be of the form (7), i.e., Vi=τi(t)∂t+ξi(t,x,u)∂x+ηi(t,x,u)∂u,i=2,3V_{i}=\tau_{i}(t)\partial_{t}+\xi_{i}(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta_{i}(t,x,u)\partial_{u},\ i=2,3. Using [V1,V2]=V3[V_{1},V_{2}]=V_{3} we find that τ2˙=τ3\dot{\tau_{2}}=\tau_{3}. Nest, it follows from [V1,V3]=−V2[V_{1},V_{3}]=-V_{2} that τ3˙=−τ2\dot{\tau_{3}}=-\tau_{2}. With these facts in hand and using the relation [V2,V3]=V1[V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1} we arrive at τ2​τ3˙−τ3​τ2˙=1\tau_{2}\dot{\tau_{3}}-\tau_{3}\dot{\tau_{2}}=1, which in turn yields equationτ22+τ2˙2=−1\tau_{2}^{2}+\dot{\tau_{2}}^{2}=-1. This equation has no real solutions, so there are no realizations of so(3) with V1=∂tV_{1}=\partial_{t}.

Turn now to the case V1=∂xV_{1}=\partial_{x}. A similar analysis yileds a unique realization of so(3)

⟨∂x,tanusinx∂x+cosx∂u,tanucosx∂x−sinx∂u⟩\langle\partial_{x},\tan u\sin x\partial_{x}+\cos x\partial_{u},\tan u\cos x\partial_{x}-\sin x\partial_{u}\rangle

However, this algebra cannot be symmetry algebra of an equation of the form (1).

Theorem 2.

There are no so(3)-invariant equations of the form (1).

In a similar way we analyze possible realizations of the algebra 𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}) and get the following assertion.

The algebras 𝑠𝑙i​(2,ℝ),(i=1,2,…,6){\it{sl}}^{i}(2,\mathbb{R}),\ (i=1,2,\dots,6) are the maximal invariance algebras of the corresponding PDEs, provided the functions FF and GG are arbitrary.

Theorem 4.

The invariant equations listed in Theorem 3 exhaust the list of all possible inequivalent PDEs (1), whose invariance algebras are semi-simple.

Proof.

It is a common knowledge that the lowest dimensional semi-simple Lie algebras admit the following isomorphisms

𝑠𝑜⁡(3)∼𝑠𝑢⁡(2)∼𝑠𝑝⁡(1),𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ)∼𝑠𝑢⁡(1,1)∼𝑠𝑜⁡(2,1)∼𝑠𝑝⁡(1,ℝ){\it{so}}(3)\sim{\it{su}}(2)\sim{\it{sp}}(1),\qquad{\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R})\sim{\it{su}}(1,1)\sim{\it{so}}(2,1)\sim{\it{sp}}(1,\mathbb{R})

(see, e.g., [2]). Hence it immediately follows that the realizations of the algebra 𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}) exhaust the set of all possible inequivalent realizations of three-dimensional semi-simple Lie algebras admitted by (1).

The next admissible dimension for classical semi-simple Lie algebras is six. There are four non-isomorphic semi-simple Lie algebras over the real number field, namely, 𝑠𝑜⁡(4){\it{so}}(4), 𝑠𝑜∗​(4){\it{so}}^{\ast}(4), 𝑠𝑜⁡(3,1){\it{so}}(3,1), and 𝑠𝑜⁡(2,2){\it{so}}(2,2). As 𝑠𝑜⁡(4)∼𝑠𝑜⁡(3)⊕𝑠𝑜⁡(3){\it{so}}(4)\sim{\it{so}}(3)\oplus{\it{so}}(3), 𝑠𝑜∗​(4)∼𝑠𝑜⁡(3)⊕𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{so}}^{\ast}(4)\sim{\it{so}}(3)\oplus{\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}), and the algebra 𝑠𝑜⁡(3,1){\it{so}}(3,1) contains 𝑠𝑜⁡(3){\it{so}}(3) as a subalgebra, there are no realization of these algebras by operator (7). Therefore 𝑠𝑜⁡(2,2){\it{so}}(2,2) is the only candidate for six-dimensional semi-simple symmetry algebra of (1).

In view of 𝑠𝑜⁡(2,2)∼𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ)⊕𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{so}}(2,2)\sim{\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus{\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}), we can choose 𝑠𝑜(2,2)=⟨Qi,Ki|i=1,2,3⟩{\it{so}}(2,2)=\langle Q_{i},K_{i}|i=1,2,3\rangle, where ⟨Q1,Q2,Q3⟩\langle Q_{1},Q_{2},Q_{3}\rangle and ⟨K1,K2,K3⟩\langle K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}\rangle are all 𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}) algebras, and [Qi,Kj]=0,(i,j=1,2,3)[Q_{i},K_{j}]=0,\ (i,j=1,2,3). Taking Q1,Q2,Q3Q_{1},\ Q_{2},\ Q_{3} to be the basis operators of the realizations of 𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}) given in the Theorem 3, and K1,K2,K3K_{1},\ K_{2},\ K_{3} be of the general form (7), we establish that realizations of 𝑠𝑙⁡(2,ℝ){\it{sl}}(2,\mathbb{R}) cannot be extended to a realization of 𝑠𝑜⁡(2,2){\it{so}}(2,2). Hence no equation of form (1) is invariant under six-dimensional semi-simple Lie algebras.

The similar reasoning yields that there are no realizations of eight-dimensional semi-simple Lie algebras 𝑠𝑙⁡(3,ℝ){\it{sl}}(3,\mathbb{R}), 𝑠𝑢⁡(3){\it{su}}(3) and 𝑠𝑢⁡(2,1){\it{su}}(2,1).

The same assertion holds true for the algebras An−1​(n>1)A_{n-1}\ (n>1), Dn​(n>1)D_{n}\ (n>1), Bn​(n≥1)B_{n}\ (n\geq 1), Cn​(n≥1)C_{n}\ (n\geq 1) and the exceptional semi-simple Lie algebras G2G_{2}, F4F_{4}, E6E_{6}, E7E_{7}, E8E_{8}.

The theorem is proved.∎

4. Classification of equations invariant under solvable Lie algebras

Using the concept of compositional series for a solvable algebra we can construct all possible realizations of solvable Lie algebras admitted by Eq.(1) starting from the one-dimensional ones and proceeding to the solvable Lie algebras of the dimension 2,3,4,…2,3,4,\ldots (for more details, see [4]).

In this section, we describe inequivalent equations of the form Eq.(1) which are invariant under solvable Lie algebras of the dimension up to four. Since equations invariant with respect to one-dimensional algebras have already been constructed, we start by analyzing two-dimensional solvable algebras.

4.1. Equations with two-dimensional Lie algebras

There are two non-isomorphic two-dimensional Lie algebras

A2.1:[V1,V2]=0,A2.2:[V1,V2]=V2.A_{2.1}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{2}]=0,\qquad A_{2.2}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{2}]=V_{2}.

As both A2.1A_{2.1} and A2.2A_{2.2} contain the algebra A1A_{1}, we can assume that the basis operator of the latter is reduced to one of the canonical forms.

We consider in detail the case of A2.1A_{2.1}, while for the case of algebra A2.2A_{2.2} we present the final results only.

Let V1=∂tV_{1}=\partial_{t} and V2V_{2} be an operator of the most general form (7)

V2=τ(t)∂t+ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂u.V_{2}=\tau(t)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u}.

Then the commutation relation implies that τ˙=ξt=ηt=0\dot{\tau}=\xi_{t}=\eta_{t}=0. Therefore τ\tau is a constant and ξ=ξ⁡(x,u),η=η⁡(x,u)\xi=\xi(x,u),\ \eta=\eta(x,u). So without any loss of generality we can put V2=ξ(x,u)∂x+η(x,u)∂uV_{2}=\xi(x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,u)\partial_{u}. Before simplifying V2V_{2} with equivalence transformations (9), we seek those equivalent transformations which preserve the basis operator V1V_{1}

V1→V¯1=T˙∂t¯+Xt∂x¯+Ut∂u¯=∂t¯.V_{1}\to\bar{V}_{1}=\dot{T}\partial_{\bar{t}}+X_{t}\partial_{\bar{x}}+U_{t}\partial_{\bar{u}}=\partial_{\bar{t}}.

Hence, T˙=1\dot{T}=1 and Xt=Ut=0X_{t}=U_{t}=0. Consequently, we can take T=t,X=X⁡(x,u)T=t,\ X=X(x,u) and U=U⁡(x,u)U=U(x,u). Performing this transformation yields

V2→V2¯=(ξXx+ηXu)∂x¯+(ξUx+ηUu)∂u¯.V_{2}\rightarrow\bar{V_{2}}=(\xi X_{x}+\eta X_{u})\partial_{\bar{x}}+(\xi U_{x}+\eta U_{u})\partial_{\bar{u}}.

If η=0\eta=0, we choose U=U⁡(u)U=U(u) and ξ\xi satisfying ξ​Xx=1\xi X_{x}=1 thus getting V2¯=∂x¯\bar{V_{2}}=\partial_{\bar{x}}. Provided η≠0\eta\neq 0, we can take XX as a solution of ξ​Xx+η​Xu=1\xi X_{x}+\eta X_{u}=1 and select UU to satisfy ξ​Ux+η​Uu=0\xi U_{x}+\eta U_{u}=0, get ∂x¯\partial_{\bar{x}} again. Thus within the action of equivalence group of Eq.(1), we get the following two-dimensional invariance algebra ⟨∂t,∂x⟩\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{x}\rangle.

Consider now the case when V1=∂xV_{1}=\partial_{x} and V2V_{2} is an operator of the form (7). Inserting V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} into the commutation relation yields V2=τ(t)∂t+ξ(t,u)∂x+η(t,u)∂uV_{2}=\tau(t)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,u)\partial_{u}. The equivalence transformation, which leaves V1V_{1} invariant, reads as

x¯=x+X⁡(t,u),u¯=U⁡(t,u)\bar{x}=x+X(t,u),\ \bar{u}=U(t,u)

with Uu≠0U_{u}\neq 0. This transformation reduces V2V_{2} to the form

V¯2=τT˙∂t¯+(τXt+ξ+ηXu)∂x¯+(τUt+ηUu)∂u¯.\bar{V}_{2}=\tau\dot{T}\partial_{\bar{t}}+(\tau X_{t}+\xi+\eta X_{u})\partial_{\bar{x}}+(\tau U_{t}+\eta U_{u})\partial_{\bar{u}}.

We consider the cases τ=0\tau=0 and τ≠0\tau\neq 0 separately.

If τ=0\tau=0 and η=0\eta=0, then V2¯=ξ∂x¯\bar{V_{2}}=\xi\partial_{\bar{x}}. If ξu≠0\xi_{u}\neq 0, choosing U=ξU=\xi yields u¯∂x¯\bar{u}\partial_{\bar{x}}. If ξu=0\xi_{u}=0 and ξt=0\xi_{t}=0, then V2¯=∂x¯\bar{V_{2}}=\partial_{\bar{x}}. And if ξu=0\xi_{u}=0 and ξt≠0\xi_{t}\neq 0, selecting T=ξT=\xi yields V2¯=t¯∂x¯\bar{V_{2}}=\bar{t}\partial_{\bar{x}}. It is straightforward to verify that the so obtained two-dimensional Lie algebra, ⟨∂x,t∂x⟩\langle\partial_{x},t\partial_{x}\rangle cannot be invariance algebras of an equation of the form (1). Now if τ=0\tau=0 and η≠0\eta\neq 0, we choose UU and XX satisfying η​Uu=1\eta U_{u}=1 and ξ+η​Xu=0\xi+\eta X_{u}=0 and get ∂u¯\partial_{\bar{u}}.

Turn next to the remaining case τ≠0\tau\neq 0. Choosing of TT, XX and UU as the solutions of the equations τ​T˙=1\tau\dot{T}=1, τ​Xt+ξ+η​Xu=0\tau X_{t}+\xi+\eta X_{u}=0 and τ​Ut+η​Uu=0\tau U_{t}+\eta U_{u}=0, respectively, we arrive at the operator ∂t¯\partial_{\bar{t}}. This yields the already known realization ⟨∂x,∂t⟩\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{t}\rangle.

This completes analysis of the realizations of the algebra A2.1A_{2.1}. The case of A2.2A_{2.2} is treated similarly.

Substituting the so obtained basis operators into the classifying equations and solving the latter yields the corresponding invariant equations.

4.2. Equations admitting three-dimensional solvable Lie algebras

We split three-dimensional solvable Lie algebras into two classes. One contains the algebras which are direct sums of lower dimensional algebras, the other includes the remaining algebras. We consider the decomposable and non-decomposable Lie algebras separately.

4.2.1 Three-dimensional decomposable algebras

There exist two non-isomorphic three-dimensional decomposable Lie algebras, A3.1A_{3.1} and A3.2A_{3.2},

A3.1=A1⊕A1⊕A1,A_{3.1}=A_{1}\oplus A_{1}\oplus A_{1},

with commutation relations

[Vi,Vj]=0​(i,j=1,2,3),[V_{i},V_{j}]=0\ (i,j=1,2,3),

and

A3.2=A2.2⊕A1,A_{3.2}=A_{2.2}\oplus A_{1},

with commutation relations

[V1,V2]=V2,[V1,V3]=0,[V2,V3]=0.[V_{1},V_{2}]=V_{2},\ [V_{1},V_{3}]=0,\ [V_{2},V_{3}]=0.

It is a common knowledge that any three-dimensional solvable Lie algebra contains two-dimensional solvable algebra as a subalgebra. So that to describe all possible realizations of three-dimensional solvable algebras admitted by Eq.(1) it suffices to consider all possible extensions of two dimensional algebras listed in Theorem 5 by vector fields V3V_{3}, of the form (7). Then for each of the so obtained realizations we simplify V3V_{3} using equivalence transformations which preserve the operators V1V_{1} and V2V_{2}. Having performed these two steps we obtain the following list of invariant equations (1):

4.2.2 Three-dimensional non-decomposable algebras

The list of inequivalent three-dimensional non-decomposable Lie algebras consists of the following seven Lie algebras (only nonzero commutation relations are given),

A3.3:[V2,V3]=V1;\displaystyle A_{3.3}:\ \ [V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1};
A3.4:[V1,V3]=V1,[V2,V3]=V1+V2;\displaystyle A_{3.4}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{3}]=V_{1},\quad[V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1}+V_{2};
A3.5:[V1,V3]=V1,[V2,V3]=V2;\displaystyle A_{3.5}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{3}]=V_{1},\quad[V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{2};
A3.6:[V1,V3]=V1,[V2,V3]=−V2;\displaystyle A_{3.6}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{3}]=V_{1},\quad[V_{2},V_{3}]=-V_{2};
A3.7:[V1,V3]=V1,[V2,V3]=qV2,(0<|q|<1);\displaystyle A_{3.7}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{3}]=V_{1},\quad[V_{2},V_{3}]=qV_{2},\ (0<|q|<1);
A3.8:[V1,V3]=−V2,[V2,V3]=V1;\displaystyle A_{3.8}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{3}]=-V_{2},\quad[V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1};
A3.9:[V1,V3]=qV1−V2,[V2,V3]=V1+qV2,(q>0).\displaystyle A_{3.9}:\ \ [V_{1},V_{3}]=qV_{1}-V_{2},\quad[V_{2},V_{3}]=V_{1}+qV_{2},\ (q>0).

All these algebras contain a two-dimensional Abelian ideal as a subalgebra. Thus, we can utilize results of classification of A2.1−A_{2.1}- invariant equations to construct Eq.(1) which admit non-decomposable three-dimensional solvable Lie algebras. As a result, we arrive at the following invariance equations:

4.3 Equations invariant under four-dimensional solvable Lie algebras

Now we perform group classification of Eq.(1) admitting four-dimensional solvable Lie algebras. To this end, we utilize the well known classification of abstract four-dimensional Lie algebras as well as the above obtained results on three-dimensional solvable algebras. For the sake of convenience we treat the cases of decomposable and non-decomposable algebras separately. Note that we skip quite cumbersome calculation details presenting the final results, symmetry algebras and invariant equations, only.

4.3.1 Equations with four-dimensional decomposable algebras

The list of non-isomorphic four-dimensional decomposable Lie algebras contains the following ten algebras:

A2.2⊕A2.2=2​A2.2,\displaystyle A_{2.2}\oplus A_{2.2}=2A_{2.2},
A3.1⊕A1=4​A1,\displaystyle A_{3.1}\oplus A_{1}=4A_{1},
A3.2⊕A1=A2.2⊕2​A1,\displaystyle A_{3.2}\oplus A_{1}=A_{2.2}\oplus 2A_{1},
A3.i⊕A1​(i=3,4,⋯,9).\displaystyle A_{3.i}\oplus A_{1}\ (i=3,4,\cdots,9).

The exhaustive list of equations (1) admitting one of the above algebras is given in Appendix A.

Each of the above algebras can be decomposed into a semi-direct sum of a three-dimensional ideal NN and a one-dimensional Lie algebra. Analysis of the commutation relations above shows that NN is of the type A3.1A_{3.1} for the algebras A4.i​(i=1,2,⋯,6)A_{4.i}\ (i=1,2,\cdots,6), of the type A3.3A_{3.3} for the algebras A4.7,A4.8,A4.9A_{4.7},\ A_{4.8},\ A_{4.9}, and of the type A3.5A_{3.5} for the algebra A4.10A_{4.10}. Thus we can utilize the already known realizations of three-dimensional solvable Lie algebras to obtain exhaustive descriptions of the four-dimensional non-decomposable solvable Lie algebras admitted by Eq.(1). The full list of inequivalent symmetry algebras and the corresponding invariant equations is given in Appendix B.

5. Classification of equations admitting quasi-local symmetries

Following the scheme developed in [20] we make use of local (Lie) symmetries of the fourth-order evolution equations (1) to obtain their non-local symmetries.

As established earlier, the most general infinitesimal operator, VV, admitted by evolution equation (1) reads as

V=τ(t)∂t+ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂uV=\tau(t)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u}

and the maximal equivalence group of Eq.(1) takes the form

t¯=T⁡(t),x¯=X⁡(t,x,u),u¯=U⁡(t,x,u),\bar{t}=T(t),\quad\bar{x}=X(t,x,u),\quad\bar{u}=U(t,x,u),

where T˙≠0\dot{T}\neq 0 and D⁡(X,U)D⁡(x,u)≠0\frac{D(X,U)}{D(x,u)}\neq 0.

If τ=0\tau=0, we have V=ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂uV=\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u} and there is an equivalence transformation (t,x,u)→(t¯,x¯,u¯)(t,x,u)\rightarrow(\bar{t},\bar{x},\bar{u}) that reduces VV to the canonical form ∂u\partial_{u} (we drop the bars). Eq.(1) now becomes

ut=F⁡(t,x,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)​ux​x​x​x+G⁡(t,x,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)u_{t}=F(t,x,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx})u_{xxxx}+G(t,x,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}) (11)

Note that the right-hand side of Eq. (11) does not depend explicitly on uu.

Differentiating (11) with respect to xx yields

ut​x=Fux​x​x​x​x+[(Fx+Fuxux​x+Fux​xux​x​x+Fux​x​xux​x​x​x)ux​x​x​x+Gx+Guxux​x+Gux​xux​x​x+Gux​x​xux​x​x​x].\begin{split}&u_{tx}=Fu_{xxxxx}+[(F_{x}+F_{u_{x}}u_{xx}+F_{u_{xx}}u_{xxx}+F_{u_{xxx}}u_{xxxx})u_{xxxx}\\[5.69054pt] &\quad\quad\ +G_{x}+G_{u_{x}}u_{xx}+G_{u_{xx}}u_{xxx}+G_{u_{xxx}}u_{xxxx}].\end{split}

Making the non-local change of variables

t¯=t,x¯=x,u¯=ux\bar{t}=t,\quad\bar{x}=x,\quad\bar{u}=u_{x} (12)

and dropping the bars, we finally get

ut=Fux​x​x​x+[(Fx+Fuux+Fuxux​x+Fux​xux​x​x)ux​x​x+Gx+Guux+Guxux​x+Gux​xux​x​x].\begin{split}&u_{t}=Fu_{xxxx}+[(F_{x}+F_{u}u_{x}+F_{u_{x}}u_{xx}+F_{u_{xx}}u_{xxx})u_{xxx}\\[5.69054pt] &\quad\quad\ +G_{x}+G_{u}u_{x}+G_{u_{x}}u_{xx}+G_{u_{xx}}u_{xxx}].\end{split} (13)

where F=F⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x)F=F(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx}) and G=G⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x)G=G(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx}).

Thus the non-local transformation (12) preserves the differential structure of the class of evolution equation (11).

Assume that Eq.(11) admits rr-parameter Lie transformation group

t′=T⁡(t,θ→),x′=X⁡(t,x,u,θ→),u′=U⁡(t,x,u,θ→)t^{\prime}=T(t,\vec{\theta}),\quad x^{\prime}=X(t,x,u,\vec{\theta}),\quad u^{\prime}=U(t,x,u,\vec{\theta}) (14)

with the vector of group parameters θ→=(θ1,…,θr)\vec{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{r}) and r≥2r\geq 2. To obtain the symmetry group of Eq.(13), we need to transform (14) according to (12). Computing the first prolongation of formulas (14), we derive the transformation rule for the first derivative of uu

ux′′=Uu​ux+UxXu​ux+Xx.u^{\prime}_{x^{\prime}}=\frac{U_{u}u_{x}+U_{x}}{X_{u}u_{x}+X_{x}}.

The transformation group (14) now reads as

t′=T⁡(t,θ→),x′=X⁡(t,x,v,θ→),u′=Uv​u+UxXv​u+Xx.t^{\prime}=T(t,\vec{\theta}),\quad x^{\prime}=X(t,x,v,\vec{\theta}),\quad u^{\prime}=\frac{U_{v}u+U_{x}}{X_{v}u+X_{x}}. (15)

with v=∂−1uv=\partial^{-1}u and U=U⁡(t,x,v,θ→)U=U(t,x,v,\vec{\theta}). Consequently, Eq.(13) admits symmetry group (15). Provided the right-hand sides of the transformation group (15) depend explicitly on the non-local variable vv, then (15) is a quasi-local symmetry of Eq.(13).

Evidently, Eq.(13) admits quasi-local symmetry iff transformation (15) satisfies

Xv≠0or∂∂v​(Uv​u+UxXv​u+Xx)≠0,X_{v}\neq 0\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\Big(\frac{U_{v}u+U_{x}}{X_{v}u+X_{x}}\Big)\neq 0,

or, equivalently

Xv≠0orXv=0,Ux​v2+Uv​v2≠0.\begin{split}X_{v}\neq 0\quad\text{or}\quad X_{v}=0,\quad\ U^{2}_{xv}+U^{2}_{vv}\neq 0.\end{split}

It is straightforward to express the above constraints in terms of the coefficients of the corresponding infinitesimal operator of group (14) and obtain the following assertion.

Theorem 6.

[20] Evolution equation (11) can be transformed to Eq.(13) admitting a quasi-local symmetry if (11) admits a Lie symmetry whose infinitesimal generator satisfies one of the following inequalities:

ξu≠0,\displaystyle\xi_{u}\neq 0, (16)
ξu=0,ηx​u2+ηu​u2≠0.\displaystyle\xi_{u}=0,\quad\eta^{2}_{xu}+\eta^{2}_{uu}\neq 0. (17)

By making a hodograph transformation

t¯=t,x¯=u,u¯=x,\bar{t}=t,\quad\bar{x}=u,\quad\bar{u}=x,

and dropping the bars, the evolution equation

ut=F⁡(t,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)​ux​x​x​x+G⁡(t,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)u_{t}=F(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx})u_{xxxx}+G(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}) (18)

can be transformed to an equation of the form (11). Hence we can get the following assertion.

Corollary 1.

Equation (18) can be reduced to an equation having a quasi-local symmetry if Eq.(18) admits a Lie symmetry satisfying one of the inequalities

ηx≠0,\displaystyle\eta_{x}\neq 0,
o​r\displaystyle or\qquad ηx=0,ξx​u2+ξx​x2≠0.\displaystyle\eta_{x}=0,\quad\xi^{2}_{xu}+\xi^{2}_{xx}\neq 0.

Based on the above reasonings, now we can formulate the algorithm for constructing evolution equations of the form (1) admitting a quasi-local symmetry.

  1. 1.

    Select all invariant equations, whose invariance algebras contain at least one operator of the form V=ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂uV=\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u}.

  2. 2.

    For each of these equations, make a suitable local equivalence transformation reducing VV to the canonical form ∂u\partial_{u}, the original equations being transformed to evolution equations of the form (11).

    item For each Lie symmetry of invariance algebra admitted by (11) check whether its infinitesimal generator satisfies one of conditions (16), (17) of Theorem 6. This analysis yields the list of evolution equations (1) that can be reduced to those admitting quasi-local symmetries.

    item Performing the non-local change of variables (12) transforms Eq.(11) to (13) which has quasi-local symmetries (15).

We processes in this way all the invariant equations obtained in Sections 3, 4 and thus obtain the list of fourth-order evolution equations (1) admitting quasi-local symmetries. Here we give the symmetry algebras of the corresponding invariant equations omitting the expressions for the functions FF and GG equations for brevity. Since we keep the same notations for Lie algebra realizations used in the previous sections, it is straightforward to deduce the explicit forms of the invariant equations given the form of its Lie symmetry algebra.

Making a suitable local equivalence transformation to reduce basis elements V=ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂uV=\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u} of each algebra listed above to the canonical form ∂u\partial_{u}, yields evolution equations of the form (11). Next, differentiating the so obtained equations with respect to xx and replacing uxu_{x} with uu yields an equation of the form (13) that admits a quasi-local symmetry. Here we consider two illustrative examples.

Example 1. Consider the algebra

𝑠𝑙4(2,ℝ)=⟨2x∂x,−x2∂x,∂x⟩{\it{sl}}^{4}(2,\mathbb{R})=\langle 2x\partial_{x},-x^{2}\partial_{x},\partial_{x}\rangle

and make a hodograph transformation

t¯=t,x¯=u,u¯=x,\bar{t}=t,\quad\bar{x}=u,\quad\bar{u}=x,

which transforms the original algebra to

⟨2u∂u,−u2∂u,∂u⟩.\langle 2u\partial_{u},-u^{2}\partial_{u},\partial_{u}\rangle.

Here we drop the bars. The invariant equation corresponding to the above algebra reads as

ut=F⁡(t,x,ω)​ux​x​x​x+3​ux​x3−4​ux​ux​x​ux​x​xux2​F​(t,x,ω)+ux​G​(t,x,ω),u_{t}=F(t,x,\omega)u_{xxxx}+\frac{3u_{xx}^{3}-4u_{x}u_{xx}u_{xxx}}{u_{x}^{2}}F(t,x,\omega)+u_{x}G(t,x,\omega),

where F,GF,\ G are arbitrary smooth functions and ω=(2​ux​ux​x​x−3​ux​x2)​ux−2\omega=(2u_{x}u_{xxx}-3u_{xx}^{2})u_{x}^{-2}. Differentiating the above equation with respect to xx and replacing uxu_{x} with uu according to (12) we arrive at the evolution equation

ut=F​ux​x​x​x+(ux​x​x+3​ux​x3−4​ux​ux​x​ux​x​xux2)​(Fx+σ​Fω)−4​u2​(ux​x2+ux​ux​x​x)−13​u​ux2​ux​x+6​ux4u3​F+ux​G+u​Gx+u​σ​Gω,\begin{split}u_{t}=&Fu_{xxxx}+(u_{xxx}+\frac{3u_{xx}^{3}-4u_{x}u_{xx}u_{xxx}}{u_{x}^{2}})(F_{x}+\sigma F_{\omega})\\[5.69054pt] &-\frac{4u^{2}(u_{xx}^{2}+u_{x}u_{xxx})-13uu_{x}^{2}u_{xx}+6u_{x}^{4}}{u^{3}}F+u_{x}G+uG_{x}+u\sigma G_{\omega},\end{split}

with ω=(2​u​ux​x−3​ux2)​u−2\omega=(2uu_{xx}-3u_{x}^{2})u^{-2} and σ=2​(u2​ux​x​x−4​u​ux​ux​x+3​ux3)​u−3\sigma=2(u^{2}u_{xxx}-4uu_{x}u_{xx}+3u_{x}^{3})u^{-3}. This equation admits the non-local symmetry transformation group

t′=t,x′=x,u′=u(θ​v+1)2,t^{\prime}=t,\quad x^{\prime}=x,\quad u^{\prime}=\frac{u}{(\theta v+1)^{2}},

with the generator −2uv∂u-2uv\partial_{u}, where θ\theta is the group parameter and v=∂−1uv=\partial^{-1}u.

Example 2. Consider the Lie algebra

2A2.22=⟨−t∂t−x∂x,∂t,∂u,eu∂u⟩2A^{2}_{2.2}=\langle-t\partial_{t}-x\partial_{x},\partial_{t},\partial_{u},\mathrm{e}^{u}\partial_{u}\rangle

and its corresponding invariant equation

ut=x3​F​(ω1,ω2)​ux​x​x​x−x3​(ux4−6​ux2​ux​x+4​ux​ux​x​x+3​ux​x2)​F​(ω1,ω2)+ux​G​(ω1,ω2),u_{t}=x^{3}F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})u_{xxxx}-x^{3}(u_{x}^{4}-6u_{x}^{2}u_{xx}+4u_{x}u_{xxx}+3u_{xx}^{2})F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})+u_{x}G(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),\\

where ω1=x⁡(ux2−ux​x)​ux−1,ω2=x2​(ux3−3​ux​ux​x+ux​x​x)​ux−1\omega_{1}=x(u_{x}^{2}-u_{xx})u_{x}^{-1},\ \omega_{2}=x^{2}(u_{x}^{3}-3u_{x}u_{xx}+u_{xxx})u_{x}^{-1} and F,GF,\ G are arbitrary smooth functions. Differentiating the above equation with respect to xx and replacing uxu_{x} with uu according to (12) yield the evolution equation

ut=x3Fux​x​x​x+3x2Fux​x​x+[x3ux​x​x−x3(ux4−6ux2ux​x+4uxux​x​x+3ux​x2)][Fω1σ1+Fω2σ2]−x2[3u4+4xu3ux−6(xux​x+3ux)u2+(−12xux2+12ux​x+4xux​x​x)u+9ux2+10xuxux​x]F+uxG+uσ1Gω1+uσ2Gω2,\begin{split}u_{t}=&x^{3}Fu_{xxxx}+3x^{2}Fu_{xxx}+[x^{3}u_{xxx}-x^{3}(u_{x}^{4}-6u_{x}^{2}u_{xx}+4u_{x}u_{xxx}+3u_{xx}^{2})][F_{\omega_{1}}\sigma_{1}\\[5.69054pt] &+F_{\omega_{2}}\sigma_{2}]-x^{2}[3u^{4}+4xu^{3}u_{x}-6(xu_{xx}+3u_{x})u^{2}+(-12xu_{x}^{2}+12u_{xx}+4xu_{xxx})u\\[5.69054pt] &+9u_{x}^{2}+10xu_{x}u_{xx}]F+u_{x}G+u\sigma_{1}G_{\omega_{1}}+u\sigma_{2}G_{\omega_{2}},\end{split}

with

ω1=x⁡(u2−ux)u,ω2=x2​(u3−3​u​ux+ux​x)u,\omega_{1}=\frac{x(u^{2}-u_{x})}{u},\ \omega_{2}=\frac{x^{2}(u^{3}-3uu_{x}+u_{xx})}{u},

and

σ1=u3+x​ux​u2−(x​ux​x+ux)​u+x​ux2u2,\displaystyle\sigma_{1}=\frac{u^{3}+xu_{x}u^{2}-(xu_{xx}+u_{x})u+xu_{x}^{2}}{u^{2}},
σ2=x⁡[2​u4+2​x​ux​u3−3​(x​ux​x+2​ux)​u2+(x​ux​x​x+2​ux​x)​u−x​ux​ux​x]u2.\displaystyle\sigma_{2}=\frac{x[2u^{4}+2xu_{x}u^{3}-3(xu_{xx}+2u_{x})u^{2}+(xu_{xxx}+2u_{xx})u-xu_{x}u_{xx}]}{u^{2}}.

The new equation admits the non-local symmetry

t′=t,x′=x,u′=u1−θ​ev,t^{\prime}=t,\quad x^{\prime}=x,\quad u^{\prime}=\frac{u}{1-\theta\mathrm{e}^{v}},

with symmetry generator

evu∂u.\mathrm{e}^{v}u\partial_{u}.

Appendix A. Equations admitting non-decomposable four-dimensional solvable Lie algebras

A4.1−A_{4.1}- invariant equations,

A4.11=⟨∂u,∂x,∂t,t∂x+x∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{1}_{4.1}=\langle\partial_{u},\partial_{x},\partial_{t},t\partial_{x}+x\partial_{u}\rangle:
F=F⁡(ux​x,ux​x​x),G=G⁡(ux​x,ux​x​x)−ux22,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=F(u_{xx},u_{xxx}),\quad G=G(u_{xx},u_{xxx})-\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{2},

F=F⁡(ux​x,ux​x​x),G=G⁡(ux​x,ux​x​x)−x22,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=F(u_{xx},u_{xxx}),\quad G=G(u_{xx},u_{xxx})-\frac{x^{2}}{2},

F=x8​F​(ω1,ω2),G=4​x2​(2​ω2−3​x​ω1)​F​(ω1,ω2)+x​G​(ω1,ω2)−12​x,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=x^{8}F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),\quad G=4x^{2}(2\omega_{2}-3x\omega_{1})F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})+xG(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})-\frac{1}{2x},

A4.21=⟨∂t,∂u,∂x,qt∂t+x∂x+(x+u)∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{1}_{4.2}=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},\partial_{x},qt\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+(x+u)\partial_{u}\rangle:
F=e(4−q)​ux​F​(ω1,ω2),G=e(1−q)​ux​G​(ω1,ω2),\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=\mathrm{e}^{(4-q)u_{x}}F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),\quad G=\mathrm{e}^{(1-q)u_{x}}G(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),
ω1=eux​ux​x,ω2=e2​ux​ux​x​x,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\omega_{1}=\mathrm{e}^{u_{x}}u_{xx},\ \omega_{2}=\mathrm{e}^{2u_{x}}u_{xxx},
A4.22=⟨∂x,∂u,∂t,t∂t+qx∂x+(t+u)∂u⟩q≠1:\displaystyle A^{2}_{4.2}=\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{u},\partial_{t},t\partial_{t}+qx\partial_{x}+(t+u)\partial_{u}\rangle\ q\neq 1:
F=ux1−4​qq−1​F​(ω1,ω2),G=G⁡(ω1,ω2)−ln⁡|ux|q−1,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=u_{x}^{\frac{1-4q}{q-1}}F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),\quad G=G(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})-\frac{\ln{|u_{x}|}}{q-1},
ω1=ux1−2​qq−1​ux​x,ω2=ux1−3​qq−1​ux​x​x,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\omega_{1}=u_{x}^{\frac{1-2q}{q-1}}u_{xx},\ \omega_{2}=u_{x}^{\frac{1-3q}{q-1}}u_{xxx},
A4.23=⟨∂x,∂u,∂t,t∂t+x∂x+(t+u)∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{3}_{4.2}=\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{u},\partial_{t},t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+(t+u)\partial_{u}\rangle:
F=1ux​x3​F​(ux,ux​x​xux​x2),G=G⁡(ux,ux​x​xux​x2)−ln⁡|ux​x|,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=\frac{1}{u_{xx}^{3}}F(u_{x},\frac{u_{xxx}}{u_{xx}^{2}}),\quad G=G(u_{x},\frac{u_{xxx}}{u_{xx}^{2}})-\ln{|u_{xx}|},
A4.24=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,qt∂t−∂x+u∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{4}_{4.2}=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},qt\partial_{t}-\partial_{x}+u\partial_{u}\rangle:

A4.25=⟨∂t,x∂u,∂u,qt∂t+x2∂x+(x+1)u∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{5}_{4.2}=\langle\partial_{t},x\partial_{u},\partial_{u},qt\partial_{t}+x^{2}\partial_{x}+(x+1)u\partial_{u}\rangle:

G=4​x6​eqx​(3​ux​x+2​x​ux​x​x)​F​(ω1,ω2)+x​eq−1x​G​(ω1,ω2),\displaystyle\qquad\qquad G=4x^{6}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{q}{x}}(3u_{xx}+2xu_{xxx})F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})+x\mathrm{e}^{\frac{q-1}{x}}G(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),

A4.26=⟨∂u,x∂u,∂t,t∂t+(q−1)x∂x+(tx+qu)∂u⟩q≠1:\displaystyle A^{6}_{4.2}=\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\partial_{t},t\partial_{t}+(q-1)x\partial_{x}+(tx+qu)\partial_{u}\rangle\ q\neq 1:
F=x4​q−5q−1​F​(ω1,ω2),G=x​G​(ω1,ω2)+x​ln⁡|x|q−1,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=x^{\frac{4q-5}{q-1}}F(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),\quad G=xG(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})+\frac{x\ln{|x|}}{q-1},
ω1=xq−2q−1​ux​x,ω2=x2​q−3q−1​ux​x​x,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\omega_{1}=x^{\frac{q-2}{q-1}}u_{xx},\ \omega_{2}=x^{\frac{2q-3}{q-1}}u_{xxx},

F=1ux​x​F​(x,ux​x​xux​x),G=G⁡(x,ux​x​xux​x)+x​ln⁡|ux​x|,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=\frac{1}{u_{xx}}F(x,\frac{u_{xxx}}{u_{xx}}),\quad G=G(x,\frac{u_{xxx}}{u_{xx}})+x\ln{|u_{xx}|},

A4.41=⟨∂u,∂x,∂t,t∂t+(t+x)∂x+(x+u)∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{1}_{4.4}=\langle\partial_{u},\partial_{x},\partial_{t},t\partial_{t}+(t+x)\partial_{x}+(x+u)\partial_{u}\rangle:

A4.56=⟨∂x,∂u,∂t,pt∂t+x∂x+u∂u⟩:\displaystyle A^{6}_{4.5}=\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{u},\partial_{t},pt\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+u\partial_{u}\rangle:
F=ux​xp−4​F​(ux,ux​x​xux​x2),G=ux​xp−1​G​(ux,ux​x​xux​x2),\displaystyle\qquad\qquad F=u_{xx}^{p-4}F(u_{x},\frac{u_{xxx}}{u_{xx}^{2}}),\quad G=u_{xx}^{p-1}G(u_{x},\frac{u_{xxx}}{u_{xx}^{2}}),
A4.57=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,t∂t+(q−p)x∂x+qu∂u⟩,p≠q:\displaystyle A^{7}_{4.5}=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},t\partial_{t}+(q-p)x\partial_{x}+qu\partial_{u}\rangle,\ p\neq q:

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
